original_question: Describe all torus decompositions that are realized by periodic two-dimensional continued fractions, where the torus decomposition records the integer-congruence types of polyhedra in a fundamental domain together with their integer distances to the cone vertex.
target_in_paper: Problem 11 (V. Arnold) in §3.3, read together with the remark immediately preceding Conjecture 10 and the algebraic-case setup [A] in §3.1.
correct_elements: The draft has correctly identified the paper's classification problem about torus decompositions arising from periodic two-dimensional continued fractions, and it already imports almost verbatim the paper's defining remark that a torus decomposition records the integer-congruence types of polyhedra in a fundamental domain together with their integer distances to the cone vertex.
missing_details: The paper is speaking specifically about periodic continued fractions in the sense of Klein, not about arbitrary multidimensional continued fractions or the Minkowski-Voronoi case (§3.3, especially the remark before Conjecture 10 and the surrounding discussion).

The relevant periodicity is the algebraic case [A]: one starts from an integer matrix A in SL(3, Z) whose characteristic polynomial is irreducible over Q and has only real roots; the corresponding arrangement/cone is algebraic, and the associated two-dimensional sail is periodic under the Dirichlet subgroup (§3.1, case [A]).
The ambient setting should be made explicit: the sail is two-dimensional because it lives in R^3 with lattice Z^3, and the cone vertex is the origin (§2.1, §3.1 [A]).
The quotient object is a 2-torus because, in case [A], the factor-sail by the Dirichlet subgroup is homeomorphic to an (n-1)-torus; here n = 3 (§3.1, case [A]).

The torus decomposition is attached to any fundamental domain for the Dirichlet subgroup action on a periodic sail; that dependence on a fundamental domain should be stated explicitly, as in the remark before Conjecture 10 (§3.3).

The technical meanings of integer congruence and integer distance are defined earlier in integer geometry via affine lattice-preserving transformations and sublattice indices, so a stand-alone version should either define or explicitly invoke those notions (Definition 1.1).

To stay paper-faithful, the question should ask for a classification/description of all realizable torus decompositions, not the weaker algorithmic decision problem of whether a given fundamental-domain type is realizable (that neighboring problem is Problem 9, not Problem 11).
The draft does not explicitly say that the problem concerns periodic two-dimensional Klein sails arising from algebraic cones; without that, the scope is slightly too implicit.
There are no homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency hypotheses in this problem; the missing paper-specific hypotheses are instead the lattice, field, and periodicity assumptions above.
refined_question: Describe exactly which torus decompositions occur for periodic two-dimensional continued fractions in the sense of Klein: namely, in the algebraic case where an irreducible matrix A in SL(3, Z) has characteristic polynomial irreducible over Q with three real roots, so that the associated two-dimensional Klein sail in R^3/Z^3 is periodic under its Dirichlet subgroup and the factor-sail is a 2-torus, determine all decompositions of that quotient torus (equivalently, of any fundamental domain) by polyhedra, recorded by the integer-congruence class of each polyhedron under affine lattice-preserving transformations and by its integer distance from the cone vertex, that can be realized.
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 11 almost exactly: the official formulation is 'Describe all torus decompositions that are realized by periodic two-dimensional continued fractions' (§3.3, Problem 11). The extra clause in the draft about recording integer-congruence types and integer distances comes from the immediately preceding remark, which defines what the paper means by a torus decomposition for a periodic sail in the Klein setting (§3.3, remark before Conjecture 10). To make the question genuinely stand-alone and paper-faithful, one must also import the algebraic periodic setup from case [A] in §3.1: periodic sails arise from algebraic cones associated with irreducible integer matrices having only real roots, the relevant symmetry group is the Dirichlet subgroup, and the quotient is a torus. The neighboring statements in §3.3 confirm that the draft should not be redirected to Problem 9 (algorithmic realizability of a given fundamental-domain type) or to Conjecture 10 (uniqueness of torus decompositions for noncongruent Klein sails); the intended target is the broader classification problem of Problem 11.
